solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Record article you haven't normally got a clue about

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the article, holding it inside
what you have not normally got is these letters in their usual order, so the words got a clue are rearranged

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A record of something you would ordinarily be clueless about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you haven't normally' scrambles GOT A CLUE into CTALOGUE, and 'about' wraps that round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A catalogue is a systematic list or register, so it serves as a record.

clue.text: Little brother wanted a cousin to show up

indicators.note: in a down clue the letters read from bottom to top
the answer is on display inside the letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A younger sibling wanted a cousin to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' hides TEDAC in wanTED A Cousin and 'up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a younger son or brother, or a junior branch of a family.

clue.text: Gather fight is what Bunter was always going to?

definitions.text: is what Bunter was always going to?

parts.note: a tuck is a fold of gathered cloth
to box is to fight with fists

explanation.surface: A question about Billy Bunter's endless appetite for food and fights.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter, a fat schoolboy in Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories, was forever raiding other boys' tuckboxes for cakes and sweets.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuckbox is a boarding-school pupil's box of food treats, the target of the greedy Bunter.

clue.text: Play Pole out of position with English amateurs

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are moved from their places

explanation.surface: A Polish player and an English one are fielded out of position by a team of amateurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Laypeople are non-professionals, people without expert training in a field.

clue.text: "Grand total to decrease?" they report sensationally

parts.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand
utter means total, complete
read as de-crease: to press clothes is to take creases out

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline asking whether a large sum will shrink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decrease' looks like reduce but reads as de-crease, take out creases, which ironing does.
explanation.definitionFit: The gutter press is the sensationalist tabloid newspapers.

clue.text: Finally wave bye bye and go out

indicators.note: the last letter of wave is taken

parts.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a bye, a run not hit by the batter
a second bye gives a second B

explanation.surface: Someone waves a last goodbye and leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: When the tide ebbs it recedes, that is, goes out.

clue.text: Stripper removing the last item: where it could happen, legally?

indicators.note: the final letter of the insect is dropped from the word

parts.note: a locust strips fields and trees bare of their leaves

explanation.surface: A striptease artist leaves off a final garment, and someone wonders where that would be legal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripper' looks like a performer but is a swarming insect that strips crops. Locus is Latin for place, used in law for the scene of an event.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal usage a locus is the place where an event such as a crime happened.

clue.text: Like a lavish meal, but with no starter to relish

indicators.note: the first letter is dropped, as a dinner served without a first course

parts.note: a slap-up meal is a lavish feast

explanation.surface: A grand dinner minus a first course, but still enjoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' suggests a first course, which suits the meal, but it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To lap up something is to enjoy it eagerly, as a cat laps milk.

clue.text: Perhaps some tests, etc, especially for handling strain

indicators.note: the shuffled letters hold the word for strain inside them
read as specially made, so the three letters are arranged anew

parts.note: to rick is to sprain or strain a joint

explanation.surface: Medical tests to diagnose a pulled muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'especially' (read as specially made) rearranges the three letters into CET, which 'for handling' wraps round the strain word. 'tests' suggests exams but means Test matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Test matches are international games of cricket, so tests are examples of the sport.

clue.text: Clock and TV close to mantelpiece? Indeed possible

parts.note: a TV set

indicators.note: the end letter of mantelpiece is taken

parts.note: yes, indeed
something on is feasible, possible

explanation.surface: A clock and television placed near the mantelpiece, if possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clock' looks like a timepiece, but is British slang for notice or see.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to clock someone is to notice them, to catch sight of them.

clue.text: Work out? People who do this probably won't!

definitions.text: Work out? People who do this probably won't!

parts.words: Work out? People who do this probably won't!
parts.note: read the answer as two words: people who run down physical training probably won't take exercise, while the whole word means work out a code

explanation.surface: A quip about people who never go to the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DECRY PT: PT is physical training, and people who decry (disparage) it are unlikely to work out at the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: To decrypt a coded message is to work out what it says.

clue.text: Roll is getting dry on the outside: I'd recommend dunking

parts.note: a bap is a soft bread roll

indicators.note: the letters for dry sit around the word is, enclosing it

parts.note: TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol, so dry
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice on softening a stale bread roll by dunking it in your tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dunking' suggests biscuits, but it is full-immersion baptism, which Baptists practise.
explanation.definitionFit: Baptists hold that baptism should be by total immersion, so one would recommend being plunged under water.

clue.text: Put up fare

definitions.meaning: in British usage, to ... a motion is to put it forward for discussion
a good ... means good food, the fare served

explanation.definitionFit: To table a proposal is to present it; the table one keeps is the food one serves.

clue.text: Diversion vital, it's impressed on PC

parts.note: an escape is a distraction or diversion from routine
key means essential, vital

explanation.surface: Some crucial distraction is stamped on a police constable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PC' looks like a police officer but is a personal computer, and 'impressed' means pressed down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Escape key on a computer keyboard is one that gets pressed by the user.

clue.text: Party with its share of famous guests?

parts.note: a celeb is a celebrity, here a famous guest
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: A party where each gets a quota of famous guests.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebration is a festive party marking an occasion.

clue.text: Spelling system that uses first half dozen letters

definitions.meaning: spelling here is the casting of spells

definitions.text: system that uses first half dozen letters
definitions.meaning: hexadecimal, ... for short, counts with digits plus the letters A to F

explanation.surface: A writing system built on just the first six letters of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A hex is a witch's curse; hex is also short for base-sixteen notation, whose extra digits are A to F.

clue.text: Manage to get on part of bed

parts.note: to head is to lead or manage
to board is to get on a vehicle

explanation.surface: Managing to get onto a piece of the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A headboard is the upright panel at the head end of a bed.

clue.text: Twice a year new driver sets out for historic part of Italy

parts.note: twice calls for a second copy of the per annum abbreviation beside the first
PA is per annum, Latin for a year
L is the learner plate on a new driver's car
to state is to set out in words

explanation.surface: A learner driver sets off on an annual trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' means the abbreviation for 'a year' (PA, per annum) is written two times.
explanation.definitionFit: The Papal States were territories in central Italy ruled by the Pope until 1870.

clue.text: Frustrating, with grant having been adjusted

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are changed around into a new order

explanation.surface: Annoying, given that the funding award was altered.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwarting someone is blocking their plans, so it means frustrating them.

clue.text: Close, around lunchtime, small joint

parts.note: at one o'clock, around lunchtime
the elbow is a joint of the arm

explanation.surface: Near lunchtime, a small joint of meat is served.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' suggests a cut of meat or a bar, but it is the arm's hinge.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at one's elbow is right beside one, near at hand.

clue.text: Bombed, if ordered up initially to attack

indicators.note: the opening letters of the two words are taken

parts.note: a fit is a sudden attack, as of coughing

explanation.surface: An air raid, if orders came to attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombed' looks military, but is slang for very drunk or stoned.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of it is slang for intoxicated, as bombed is.

clue.text: Female at the time needing to lose weight

indicators.note: the letter for weight is dropped from the word

parts.note: when means at the time that

explanation.surface: A woman who at that point had to slim down.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen is a female bird, and in Scots or slang a woman.

clue.text: Carrying an unpleasant smell, another's banned from table tennis

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell

indicators.note: the second smell is excluded from the game's name

parts.note: ping-pong is another name for table tennis
another unpleasant smell is a pong

explanation.surface: A smelly player is barred from table tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: HUM and PONG are both British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: To hump something is British slang for lugging or carrying a heavy load.

clue.text: Stick with short answer: you could be in the doghouse there?

definitions.text: you could be in the doghouse there?

parts.note: a bat is a stick used to hit a ball
terse means short, curt

explanation.surface: Give a curt reply and you might find yourself in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the doghouse' means in disgrace, but here it is literal: BATTERSEA Dogs Home is London's famous shelter for stray dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Battersea, in south London, is home to the well-known dogs' rescue home, literally a house for dogs.

clue.text: Irish town you might have been in first? Oddly, no

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are refused, leaving the even ones

explanation.surface: A question about whether you reached an Irish town first, answered no.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in the west of Ireland.

clue.text: Totter backwards, avoiding a married uncle or brother

indicators.note: one of the letters for married is left out
the word for the adder is read in reverse

parts.note: one who tots up figures is a summer, someone who adds sums
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: Someone staggers backwards, steering clear of a married relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Totter' looks like a stagger but is one who tots up: SUMMER, which 'backwards' turns into REMMUS; dropping one M leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Remus is Uncle Remus of the Brer Rabbit tales and the twin brother of Romulus, legendary founders of Rome.

clue.text: The French department giving a few extra marks

indicators.note: an additional letter is slipped into the word

parts.note: some means a few
M is short for marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A French civil service office awarding bonus points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' looks like a pointer to a French word, but it belongs to the definition: Somme is a département of France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Somme is a département of northern France, named after its river.

clue.text: Spaniard maybe in East London semi, soon to move

parts.note: a Cockney from East London drops the h, so half, semi, becomes 'alf

indicators.note: the letters of soon are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A Spanish man in a semi-detached house in East London is about to move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'semi' suggests a house; it means half, which a Cockney (East Londoner) says as 'ALF. 'to move' rearranges SOON as ONSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfonso is a Spanish man's name, borne by several kings of Spain.

clue.text: Passes round Kansas

parts.note: O is round in shape
KS is the postal abbreviation for Kansas

explanation.surface: Mountain passes surrounding the state of Kansas.
explanation.definitionFit: OKs are approvals; to OK something is to pass it.

clue.text: Two posh male guards deliver something metallic

indicators.note: the outer letters surround the word for deliver, as guards encircle a prisoner

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals
to rid is to free or deliver from something
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: A pair of upper-class men protect a delivery of something made of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deliver' means free from, as in deliver us from evil.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridium is a hard, dense metallic element of the platinum group.

clue.text: Is foolish to finish with Times publication

parts.note: to do someone in is to finish them off
TES, the Times Educational Supplement, was published by the Times

explanation.surface: Someone is daft enough to end things with a Times publication.
explanation.definitionFit: To dote can mean to be silly or feeble-minded, as in one's dotage.

clue.text: Religious congregation highly impatient after failing to be heard

indicators.note: the two words run together are said aloud and sound like the answer

parts.note: agog (highly impatient) placed after sin (a failing) gives sin-agog, said aloud as the answer

explanation.surface: A worshipper is eager to be heard after a lapse.
explanation.definitionFit: A synagogue is a Jewish congregation as well as its building.
